name: Clockify
tagline: Time tracker and timesheet app for teams, with apps on every platform and 80+ integrations

pricing.notes: Standard at $6.99 per seat billed monthly, $5.49 billed annually. Basic $4.99, Pro $9.99, Enterprise $14.99 monthly. The free tier is unlimited tracking for up to 5 users, which is the real competitor to any DIY build.

verdictSummary: A personal timer with projects, a weekly timesheet and a CSV export is a weekend, and for one freelancer that is genuinely the whole product. Two things stop it being a yes. Clockify's free tier already covers up to 5 users with unlimited tracking, so the subscription you would be killing is the team half · approvals, locked periods, admin controls and billable rates for people who will not touch a terminal. And the reason anyone's team actually logs time is that the timer is already in front of them, in a desktop app with idle detection, on a phone, and as a browser extension button inside Jira and Trello. Rebuilding the timer is easy. Rebuilding the habit is not.
coreLoopDIY: Start and stop a timer against a project from a menu bar or the terminal, review the week as a timesheet grid, and export it to CSV.
requirements: an always-on box if more than one device should see the same timer
macOS for the menu bar and idle detection as specified
whatYouLose: desktop, mobile and browser-extension timers, so the button is wherever the work is
idle detection and the auto tracker that catches the hours you forgot to start
team timesheets, approvals and locked periods for people who are not technical
80+ integrations that put a start button inside Jira, Trello, Asana and GitHub
billable rates, invoicing, expenses and scheduled reports on the paid tiers
moatType: team workflow + a timer on every surface
whyPeopleStillPay: Nobody pays Clockify for the stopwatch. They pay because five people who did not build it will use it every day without being asked twice, because the hours end up somewhere an approver can sign off, and because the free tier stops exactly where a growing team starts caring about admin. A local timer solves the tracking problem for the one person who wrote it and creates a data-collection problem for everyone else on the team.

prompt:
Build me a personal time tracker to replace Clockify, for macOS. Requirements:

- Node + Express + better-sqlite3, one process on localhost:4830, plus a
  SwiftBar plugin that shows the running timer in my menu bar and refreshes
  every 10 seconds. No accounts, no telemetry, the sqlite file is the truth.
- Projects with a name, client and colour, defined in projects.json and synced
  into the db on boot. Entries store description, project, started_at and
  ended_at as ISO-8601 UTC.
- CLI first, because that is where I live: `t start "ABC-1 fix login" acme`,
  `t stop`, `t status`, `t edit last "better description"`. Starting a timer
  stops the running one, so two can never run at once.
- Idle detection: a launchd agent polls `ioreg -c IOHIDSystem` for HIDIdleTime
  every minute and, if I was idle over 10 minutes while a timer ran, asks on
  the next CLI call whether to trim those minutes or keep them.
- The web page is a weekly timesheet grid: days as columns, projects as rows,
  hours as "3h 25m", editable cells that write entries back, arrow keys to
  move between weeks.
- CSV export for a date range with date, project, client, description and
  decimal hours, saved to ~/Timesheets/YYYY-MM-DD-to-YYYY-MM-DD.csv.
- Out of scope: multi-user, approvals, invoicing, mobile. No auth of any kind.
- README: installing the SwiftBar plugin and loading the launchd agent, and a
  note that macOS prompts for permissions the first time each one runs.
